headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors: Haystack can ingest MCP/REST content while Plandex can act on it with shell and filesystem writes.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Haystack exposes REST APIs and MCP servers and has broad network egress, so it can ingest attacker-controlled content. Plandex reads from stdin/stdout and project files, and its review-then-apply flow can be steered if Haystack output is treated as instructions. The pair has a direct bridge via MCP/outputs, so prompt injection is plausible by default.
conditions: IF Haystack ingests untrusted web or API content and forwards it into Plandex prompts, injection is possible.
IF Plandex auto-apply is enabled, malicious instructions in Haystack output can be executed without manual review.
mitigations: Disable auto-apply in Plandex.
Insert a provenance filter between Haystack and Plandex.
Strip instructions from retrieved content before passing it onward.
Require human review of all Haystack-generated prompt text.
requires-engineering: add content-signing or provenance tags across the bridge.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Haystack touches anonymous usage statistics and has broad network egress; Plandex reads and writes a project directory plus plan-local sandbox and can send data to a model provider. There is no shared filesystem explicitly stated, but if the pair is wired through the same workspace or MCP bridge, source code or retrieved content can leak to external services through either agent.
conditions: IF Haystack is connected to the same workspace or secrets-bearing corpus as Plandex, retrieved content can be exposed.
IF Plandex sends project files to a model provider while Haystack surfaces those files in prompts, leakage expands beyond one agent.
mitigations: Keep Haystack and Plandex on separate workspaces.
Exclude secrets from Haystack retrieval indexes.
Disable broad egress where possible.
Use redaction before any cross-agent handoff.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention policies.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Plandex can write the filesystem, modify git state, execute shell, and spawn subprocesses. Haystack can call REST APIs and MCP servers, so if it is configured to write into the same project or trigger tools through MCP, both agents can mutate shared state without any locking mechanism being documented. That overlap makes destructive write conflicts likely.
conditions: IF Haystack writes to the same repository or workspace that Plandex edits, concurrent mutations can collide.
IF both agents operate on git state without external locking, commits or staged changes can be overwritten.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Serialize write access with a lock file.
Disable one agent's write path during the other's run.
Review staged git diffs before apply.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Haystack is a search-RAG agent that can generate retrieved facts, and Plandex is a coding agent with review-then-apply behavior plus shell and git authority. If Plandex treats Haystack output as authoritative, a bad retrieval or hallucinated fact can cascade into code changes, shell actions, or commits. The downstream blast radius is larger than a single document.
conditions: IF Plandex consumes Haystack output without independent verification, erroneous facts can become code or shell actions.
IF Haystack retrieves stale or malicious content, Plandex may propagate it into commits or applied patches.
mitigations: Require source citations for every Haystack claim.
Add a verification step before Plandex apply.
Limit Plandex to dry-run mode for cross-agent tasks.
Compare Haystack outputs against primary sources.
requires-engineering: implement automated fact-checking gates.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source and the profiles do not show a clear residency or certification mismatch. Haystack touches anonymous usage statistics, while Plandex touches source code and model-provider keys, but no PHI, EU-only data, or conflicting retention policy is documented. Compliance risk is therefore limited and mostly contingent on deployment choices not shown here.
conditions: IF either agent is deployed on regulated data not listed in the profiles, compliance risk increases.
IF the operator routes EU PII or PHI through either agent, additional controls are required.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair.
Document retention settings for both tools.
Review vendor DPAs before deployment.
Separate environments by data class.
requires-engineering: add residency-aware routing.
